contentBody: **How should you name chatbot role-play when you present?**
option.1: Call it simulated feedback, not proof that users already love the offer
option.2: Call it a completed survey of everyone in the intended market as a whole
option.3: Hide the source and end with a funding story instead of one clear ask
option.4: Flip through several visual themes and treat that flip as the evidence
answerExplanation: Say simulated feedback when that is the source. Do not claim users love the offer, hide the source, or replace the story with extra themes.

contentBody: **Two findings point different ways. What belongs in the change log?**
option.1: Only the finding that matches the extra feature you already wanted to add
option.2: Neither finding, so the presentation can skip mentioning the conflict at all
option.3: Both findings and the MVP rule you used to decide the tie-break on the page
option.4: A taste-only note with no source, used to replace both of those findings
answerExplanation: If two findings fight, record both and show the MVP tie-break. Dropping one side, skipping the conflict, or replacing them with taste is not a trustworthy log.

contentBody: **How do you state a trade-off without it sounding like an excuse?**
option.1: Name only the downside and skip saying what the choice was meant to protect
option.2: Name both sides, link the choice to time or MVP, and name the remaining risk
option.3: Promise that the skipped feature is already live so that nobody has to worry
option.4: Replace the spoken trade-off with adjectives such as seamless and revolutionary
answerExplanation: Name what you chose and what you gave up, tie it to time or the MVP, and name the risk you still own. An apology, a false live claim, or adjectives is not that pattern.
